What is Day Trading?

Published by TradeHQ. Site creator and editorial approach: Anuga Weerasinghe. This page has no recorded editorial review date.

DETAILED DEFINITION

Day trading describes opening and closing positions within the same trading day. Fully closing a position removes that position’s later price exposure, but an intended close can be interrupted by a halt, outage or liquidity shortage. Frequent transactions can make spread, commission and slippage important even when gross gains look positive. Neither full-time screen use nor a fixed number of transactions establishes competence or profitability. Margin and account requirements depend on current venue, broker and jurisdiction rules. This entry does not assert a universal retail loss rate. TradeHQ is a virtual spot simulator, not a brokerage or a margin account.

HOW IT WORKS

Day trading means opening and closing positions within a trading day. It reduces exposure to overnight moves while retaining intraday price, execution and cost risks; no universal loss rate is asserted.

KEY POINTS
All positions opened and closed within the same trading day
Published research and broker disclosures often report high loss rates among retail day traders; the exact rate varies by market, time period, and sample
Real account margin and day-trading requirements depend on current rules, broker and jurisdiction
💡 WHY THIS MATTERS

Compare the time demands and assumptions of swing and intraday examples; practice profit alone does not establish readiness for real-money trading.

Worked exercise and its limits

A hypothetical 100-share purchase at $20 and sale at $20.10 gains $10 gross. If total modeled costs are $12, the net result is a $2 loss. Closing the position removes its later price exposure, but does not establish that repeated intraday trading is profitable.

References and scope
SEC Investor.gov — market, limit and stop order mechanics
SEC Investor.gov — leveraged investing risks
